raw_text: Nonburnable Fuel Type (NB): Nonburnable fuel models are included to provide consistency in how nonburnable portions of the landscape are displayed on a fuel model map. In all NB fuel models there is no fuel load — wildland fire will not spread. There are five nonburnable designations: Urban or suburban development (NB1) where the area must not support wildland fire spread — note that structure ignition may still occur via house-to-house transmission or firebrands during a wildland fire incident, but this is not modeled by fire behavior fuel models; if sufficient fuel vegetation surrounds structures such that wildland fire spread is possible, a vegetative fuel model should be used instead. Snow and ice (NB2) covering land permanently or seasonally — areas with seasonal snow may carry two fuel model designations, one for snow-covered periods and one for fire season. Agricultural land maintained in a nonburnable condition (NB3) such as irrigated annual crops or mowed orchards — however many agricultural areas are not maintained as nonburnable, for example grass allowed to grow beneath vines or crops allowed to cure before harvest, and in those cases a vegetative fuel model should be used. Open water (NB8) including lakes, rivers, and oceans. Bare ground (NB9) including gravel pits, arid deserts with little vegetation, sand dunes, rock outcroppings, and beaches. When a cell_state record shows fire_intensity of zero and vegetaion_cover_evc consistent with any of these conditions, NB classification should be considered before attempting fuel model selection.

Grass Fuel Type (GR): The primary carrier of fire in GR fuel models is grass. Grass fuels can vary from heavily grazed grass stubble or sparse natural grass to dense grass more than 6 feet tall. Fire behavior varies from moderate spread rate and low flame length in the sparse grass models to extreme spread rate and flame length in the tall grass models. All GR fuel models are dynamic, meaning that their live herbaceous fuel load shifts from live to dead as a function of live herbaceous moisture content. The effect of live herbaceous moisture content on spread rate and intensity is strong. This is a critical operational distinction: when live herbaceous moisture is high (plant is green, NDVI high), fire spread is suppressed; as the grass cures and moisture drops, fire behavior increases rapidly. GR models span two climate regimes. Arid to semiarid climate models (extinction moisture 15%) include GR1 through GR7 and represent grasses in rainfall-deficient summer environments. Subhumid to humid climate models (extinction moisture 30-40%) include GR3, GR5, GR6, GR8, and GR9 and represent grasses where rainfall is adequate across seasons. GR1 represents short, sparse, or heavily grazed grass — spread rate moderate, flame length low — and can be applied in either climate regime due to its generally low behavior. GR2 is low load dry climate grass with a more continuous fuelbed than GR1. GR3 is low load, very coarse, humid climate grass about 2 feet deep. GR4 is moderate load dry climate grass about 2 feet deep. GR5 is low load humid climate grass, denser than GR3 but shallower. GR6 is moderate load humid climate grass — notable because it uses a heat content of 9000 BTU/lb rather than the standard 8000, reflecting its fuel composition. GR7 is high load dry climate grass about 3 feet tall with very high spread rate and very high flame length. GR8 is high load, very coarse, humid climate grass 3-5 feet tall where spread rate and flame length can be extreme if fully cured. GR9 is very heavy, coarse, continuous humid climate grass 5-8 feet tall — spread rate and flame length are extreme under cured conditions. When reasoning about a GR cell: fuel_moisture maps to dead fuel moisture scenario; vegtation_greeness_ndvi maps to live herbaceous moisture and degree of curing; wind_speed_mps is the dominant driver of rate of spread increase; region and humidity_pct inform climate regime selection between dry and humid GR variants.

Grass-Shrub Fuel Type (GS): The primary carrier of fire in GS fuel models is grass and shrubs combined — both components are important in determining fire behavior. GS fuel models apply when shrubs cover up to approximately 50 percent of the site and grass is also present and contributing to fire spread. All GS fuel models are dynamic, meaning that their live herbaceous fuel load shifts from live to dead as a function of live herbaceous moisture content. The effect of live herbaceous moisture content on spread rate and intensity is strong and depends on the relative amount of grass versus shrub load in the fuel model. As with GR models, NDVI is a useful proxy for the degree of herbaceous curing and therefore for expected fire behavior intensity. GS models also span two climate regimes. Arid to semiarid climate models with extinction moisture of 15% include GS1 and GS2. GS1 represents shrubs about 1 foot high with low grass load — spread rate moderate, flame length low. GS2 represents shrubs 1 to 3 feet high with moderate grass load — spread rate high, flame length moderate. Subhumid to humid climate models with extinction moisture of 30-40% include GS3 and GS4. GS3 has moderate grass and shrub load with average depth less than 2 feet — spread rate high, flame length moderate. GS4 has heavy grass and shrub load with depth greater than 2 feet — spread rate high, flame length very high. GS4 has by far the highest fine fuel load of the GS models at 12.4 tons per acre compared to 1.35-3.0 for the others, and its fire behavior reflects this. When reasoning about a GS cell: vegetaion_cover_evc showing mixed grass-shrub with shrub coverage up to 50% is the primary classifier into GS rather than GR or SH; fuel_moisture and vegtation_greeness_ndvi together determine the live-to-dead herbaceous transfer and therefore current fire behavior potential; wind_speed_mps drives rate of spread increase; region and humidity_pct distinguish dry versus humid GS variants.

Shrub Fuel Type (SH): The primary carrier of fire in SH fuel models is live and dead shrub twigs and foliage in combination with dead and down shrub litter. Shrubs cover at least 50 percent of the site; grass is sparse to nonexistent. A small amount of herbaceous fuel may be present in some models. SH1 and SH9 are dynamic models where live herbaceous fuel load shifts between live and dead based on moisture content; all other SH models are static. The effect of live herbaceous moisture content on spread rate and flame length can be strong in those dynamic models, but in static SH models fire behavior is driven primarily by the dead fuel moisture scenario. SH models span two climate regimes. Arid to semiarid climate models with extinction moisture of 15% include SH1, SH2, SH5, and SH7. SH1 is low load dry climate shrub with fuelbed depth about 1 foot — spread rate very low, flame length very low. SH2 is moderate load dry climate shrub, depth about 1 foot, no grass present — spread rate low, flame length low. SH5 is heavy load dry climate shrub 4-6 feet deep — spread rate very high, flame length very high. SH7 is very heavy load dry climate shrub also 4-6 feet deep — spread rate is lower than SH5 but flame length is similar, both very high, reflecting different fuel structure. Subhumid to humid climate models with extinction moisture of 30-40% include SH3, SH4, SH6, SH8, and SH9. SH3 is moderate load humid climate shrub possibly with pine overstory, 2-3 feet deep — spread rate low, flame length low. SH4 is low to moderate load humid climate timber-shrub possibly with pine overstory, about 3 feet deep — spread rate high, flame length moderate, notable because despite relatively low fine fuel load it produces high spread rate. SH6 is dense humid climate shrub with little herbaceous fuel, about 2 feet deep — spread rate high, flame length high. SH8 is dense humid climate shrub with little herbaceous fuel, about 3 feet deep — spread rate high, flame length high. SH9 is very high load humid climate shrub with dense finely branched shrubs 4-6 feet tall with significant fine dead fuel — spread rate high, flame length very high, and it is dynamic due to some herbaceous component. When reasoning about a SH cell: vegetaion_cover_evc showing dominant shrub coverage over 50% with sparse grass is the primary classifier into SH; fuel depth implied by cover and height is the key differentiator among SH sub-models at the fuel type level; fuel_moisture maps to dead fuel moisture scenario and is the primary behavioral driver for static SH models; wind_speed_mps drives spread rate increase; region distinguishes dry versus humid SH variants.

Timber-Understory Fuel Type (TU): The primary carrier of fire in TU fuel models is forest litter in combination with herbaceous or shrub fuels. TU models represent the hybrid zone where a forest canopy exists but the understory — grass, shrubs, or mixed vegetation — contributes meaningfully to surface fire behavior alongside the litter layer. TU1 and TU3 contain live herbaceous load and are dynamic — their live herbaceous fuel load is allocated between live and dead as a function of live herbaceous moisture content. The effect of live herbaceous moisture content on spread rate and intensity is strong in those models and depends on the relative amount of grass and shrub load. All other TU models are static. TU models span a range of climate conditions. TU1 is low load dry climate timber-grass-shrub with extinction moisture of 20% — spread rate low, flame length low. It represents open forest with a sparse grass or shrub understory. TU2 is moderate load humid climate timber-shrub with extinction moisture of 30% — spread rate moderate, flame length low. TU3 is moderate load humid climate timber-grass-shrub with extinction moisture of 30% — spread rate high, flame length moderate. It is notable that TU3 produces higher spread rates than TU2 despite similar total load, due to its herbaceous component and dynamic nature. TU4 is dwarf conifer with understory — short conifer trees with grass or moss understory — with the lowest extinction moisture of any TU model at 12%, indicating a very dry fuel complex that ignites readily. TU4 has the highest characteristic SAV of any model in the entire dataset at 2216 1/ft, reflecting the fine fuel structure of short conifers. Spread rate and flame length are both moderate. TU5 is very high load dry climate timber-shrub with extinction moisture of 25% — heavy forest litter with a shrub or small tree understory — spread rate moderate, flame length moderate despite the very high total fuel load, because the load is dominated by coarse fuels with lower reactivity. When reasoning about a TU cell: vegetaion_cover_evc showing forest cover with a contributing understory layer is the classifier into TU versus TL; if the understory is grass or herbaceous and the cell shows moderate NDVI, TU1 or TU3 are candidates depending on climate; for dense shrub understory under forest, TU2 or TU5 are candidates; fuel_moisture is the primary behavioral driver for static TU models; wind_speed_mps drives rate of spread.

Timber Litter Fuel Type (TL): The primary carrier of fire in TL fuel models is dead and down woody fuel — needle litter, leaf litter, and downed logs beneath a forest canopy. Live fuel, if present, has little effect on fire behavior in TL models. All TL models are static. TL models generally produce lower spread rates and flame lengths than grass or shrub fuel types, but they are important because surface fire behavior in TL fuelbeds drives crown fire initiation models — increased precision in TL surface fire intensity prediction leads to increased precision in crown fire hazard assessment. TL models are differentiated primarily by litter type (conifer needle versus broadleaf leaf), fuel load, compactness, and whether coarse fuels such as downed logs are present. TL1 is low load compact conifer litter 1-2 inches deep — spread rate very low, flame length very low. It may represent recently burned forest where litter has been partially consumed. TL2 is low load compact broadleaf litter — spread rate very low, flame length very low. TL3 is moderate load conifer litter with light coarse fuels — spread rate very low, flame length low. TL4 is moderate load fine litter with small diameter downed logs — spread rate low, flame length low. TL5 is high load conifer litter with light slash or mortality fuel — spread rate low, flame length low. TL6 is moderate load broadleaf litter less compact than TL2 — spread rate moderate, flame length low. TL7 is heavy load forest litter with larger diameter downed logs — spread rate low, flame length low despite the large log component, because logs are coarse fuels with slow ignition. TL8 is moderate load long-needle pine litter, notable for its high extinction moisture of 35% indicating it burns under relatively moist conditions — spread rate moderate, flame length low. TL9 is very high load fluffy broadleaf litter or heavy needle-drape — spread rate moderate, flame length moderate. TL8 and TL9 have the highest extinction moisture in the TL group at 35%, reflecting their humid-climate or structurally open fuel conditions. When reasoning about a TL cell: vegetaion_cover_evc showing closed forest canopy with little understory vegetation is the classifier into TL; fuel_moisture is the primary behavioral driver since all TL models are static; wind_speed_mps still influences spread rate but TL fuelbeds are generally less wind-responsive than grass types; the presence or absence of downed logs and litter type (needle vs broadleaf) further differentiates TL sub-models at a finer reasoning level.

Slash-Blowdown Fuel Type (SB): The primary carrier of fire in SB fuel models is activity fuel — logging slash and debris from timber harvest — or blowdown debris from wind damage events. Forested areas with heavy tree mortality, such as from insect kill or disease, may also be modeled with SB fuel models when the dead and down fuel load is sufficiently elevated. All SB models are static. SB models are characterized by high total fuel loads dominated by dead and down woody material across multiple size classes, and they produce a wide range of fire behavior depending on fuel arrangement and loading. SB1 is low load activity fuel where fine fuel load is 10-20 tons per acre weighted toward 1-3 inch diameter class, depth less than 1 foot — spread rate moderate, flame length low. SB2 covers moderate load activity fuel or low load blowdown — fine fuel load 7-12 tons per acre evenly distributed across size classes, depth about 1 foot, blowdown scattered with many trees still standing — spread rate moderate, flame length moderate. SB3 covers high load activity fuel or moderate blowdown — fine fuel load 7-12 tons per acre weighted toward the finest size class (0-0.25 inch diameter), depth more than 1 foot, blowdown trees compacted near ground — spread rate high, flame length high. The fine fuel weighting toward small diameter fuels in SB3 produces higher spread rates than SB2 despite similar total load. SB4 is high load total blowdown where fuelbed is not compacted and most foliage and fine fuel remain attached to downed trees — spread rate very high, flame length very high. SB4's high spread rate despite similar load to SB3 reflects the elevated and aerated nature of recently downed fuel with attached foliage. When reasoning about a SB cell: vegetaion_cover_evc showing post-harvest or post-blowdown conditions with heavy downed woody debris is the primary classifier into SB; fuel_moisture is the primary behavioral driver for all static SB models; wind_speed_mps drives spread rate; the distinction between activity fuel and blowdown affects fuelbed structure and therefore the appropriate SB sub-model, but at the fuel type level SB classification is appropriate for any high-load downed woody fuel scenario.

Dynamic Fuel Model Operation: In the standard fire behavior fuel model set, all fuel models that have a live herbaceous component are dynamic. A dynamic fuel model transfers live herbaceous load between the live and dead categories based on the live herbaceous moisture content. This transfer is the single most important concept for reasoning about grass-dominated fuel types in a cell_state context. The transfer rules are as follows. If live herbaceous moisture content is 120 percent or higher, the herbaceous fuels are fully green and all herbaceous load stays in the live category at the given moisture content — fire behavior in this state is suppressed by the high moisture. If live herbaceous moisture content is 30 percent or lower, the herbaceous fuels are considered fully cured and all herbaceous load is transferred to the dead herbaceous category — fire behavior in this state is at its maximum potential for the given fuel model. If live herbaceous moisture content is between 30 and 120 percent, then the fraction of herb load transferred to dead is interpolated linearly. For example, at 75 percent live herbaceous moisture (halfway between 30 and 120), half the herbaceous load transfers to dead. The transferred load is not placed in the standard dead 1-hour timelag class but instead creates a separate dead herbaceous class that preserves the surface-area-to-volume ratio of the original live herbaceous component — this makes the transferred fuel more reactive than coarser dead fuels. The moisture content of the new dead herbaceous class is set equal to the dead 1-hour timelag moisture for simplicity. In a cell_state context, live herbaceous moisture content is not directly measured but can be estimated from vegtation_greeness_ndvi using the NDVI interpretation table in the field mappings artifact. The degree of herbaceous curing — the observable field correlate — can also be used directly via the curing table: observed 50% curing corresponds to 75% live herbaceous moisture, meaning half the herbaceous load has transferred to dead. Dynamic fuel models affected by this logic include all GR models, all GS models, SH1, SH9, TU1, and TU3. Static models including all TL, SB, and most SH and TU models do not undergo this transfer and their fuel load distribution is fixed regardless of live moisture content. A fire behavior processor that does not implement dynamic fuel model logic will leave all herbaceous load in the live category regardless of moisture, causing significant underprediction of fire behavior for cured or partly cured grass fuelbeds.

Fuel Model Selection Procedure: Selecting the appropriate fuel type from a cell_state record follows a four-step process derived from the standard fuel model selection guide. Step 1 — Determine the fire-carrying fuel type by identifying which stratum of surface fuels is most likely to carry the fire. Even in a forested area, if the forest canopy is open and grass is present in the understory, grass rather than needle litter may carry the fire, in which case a GR model should be considered rather than TL. The fire-carrying fuel type options are: grass (GR), grass-shrub mixture (GS), shrub (SH), timber litter under forest canopy (TL), timber with grass or shrub understory (TU), and slash or blowdown (SB). If no fuel is present or fuel cannot carry fire, classify as nonburnable (NB). vegetaion_cover_evc is the primary cell_state field for this determination. Step 2 — Determine the dead fuel extinction moisture, which defines the moisture content at which fire will no longer spread. This parameter is generally associated with climate: arid to semiarid regions where rainfall is deficient in summer use extinction moisture of 15%; semiarid to subhumid regions use 20-25%; subhumid to humid regions where rainfall is adequate in all seasons use 30-40%. The region field and humidity_pct in cell_state inform this determination. Step 3 — Note the general depth, compactness, and size of the fuel and the relative amount of live vegetation. Fuelbed depth and fine fuel load are the key differentiators within a fuel type at the sub-model level. For fuel type level reasoning, the key distinction is whether the fuel complex is sparse or dense, and whether live vegetation is a meaningful component of the fire-carrying fuel. vegtation_greeness_ndvi informs live vegetation status. Step 4 — Do not restrict selection by fuel model name or geographic label. A model named for a specific vegetation type can apply in many vegetation types if the fuel structure matches. After selecting a fuel type, the predicted fire behavior should be validated against expected behavior given wind speed, fuel moisture, and regional context. Important note: the fuel model set described in RMRS-GTR-153 is designed for predicting surface fire behavior at the flaming front only, not residual combustion after the flaming front passes. The model assumes homogeneous and continuous fuels. Methods for addressing heterogeneous or discontinuous fuels are available in fire modeling systems but are outside the scope of this document.

Moisture Scenario Application: Standard moisture scenarios were developed to facilitate comparison of fire behavior fuel models with each other and with the original 13 fuel models. Dead fuel moisture scenarios D1 through D4 and live fuel moisture scenarios L1 through L4 can be combined into 16 unique moisture scenario combinations. However fire behavior predicted with fuel models without a live fuel component is not affected by the live moisture scenario — only models with live herbaceous or live woody load are affected. Dead fuel moisture scenarios: D1 (Very Low) uses 1-hr moisture of 3%, 10-hr of 4%, 100-hr of 5%. D2 (Low) uses 1-hr of 6%, 10-hr of 7%, 100-hr of 8%. D3 (Moderate) uses 1-hr of 9%, 10-hr of 10%, 100-hr of 11%. D4 (High) uses 1-hr of 12%, 10-hr of 13%, 100-hr of 14%. Live fuel moisture scenarios: L1 (Fully Cured) uses live herbaceous moisture of 30% and live woody moisture of 60%. L2 (Two-thirds Cured) uses live herbaceous of 60% and live woody of 90%. L3 (One-third Cured) uses live herbaceous of 90% and live woody of 120%. L4 (Fully Green) uses live herbaceous of 120% and live woody of 150%. In cell_state reasoning, fuel_moisture is the primary input to dead scenario selection. temperature_c and humidity_pct provide contextual support when fuel_moisture is uncertain — high temperature and low humidity push toward D1/D2, high humidity pushes toward D3/D4. vegtation_greeness_ndvi is the primary input to live scenario selection for dynamic fuel models. The standard comparison baseline used throughout the document is moisture scenario D2L2 — low dead fuel moisture with two-thirds cured live herbaceous — at a midflame wind speed of 5 miles per hour and zero slope. Fire behavior adjective class descriptions (Very Low through Extreme) for both rate of spread and flame length are defined at this baseline condition.

Crosswalk from Original 13 Fuel Models: The original 13 fire behavior fuel models (numbered 1-13) developed by Albini (1976) and described by Anderson (1982) remain valid and available. The new standard set described in RMRS-GTR-153 does not repeat any of the original 13 models but is designed to stand alone. For users or systems that previously used the original 13 models, crosswalk tables provide guidance on equivalent or comparable models in the new set. Key crosswalk relationships: Original model 1 (Short Grass) maps most closely to GR1 or GR2 depending on load and continuity. Original model 2 (Timber Grass and Understory) maps to GR2, GR3, GR4, GS1, or GS2 depending on shrub component and climate. Original model 3 (Tall Grass) maps to GR7, GR8, or GR9 depending on load and climate — note that new grass models are dynamic while original model 3 is static, so direct comparison requires live herbaceous moisture of 30% or less. Original model 4 (Chaparral) maps to SH5, SH6, SH7, SH8, or SH9 depending on load and climate. Original model 5 (Brush) maps to SH1, SH2, GS2 depending on grass component. Original model 6 (Dormant Brush) maps to SH1, SH2, SH3, SH4. Original model 7 (Southern Rough) maps to SH5, SH6, SH7. Original models 8, 9, 10 (Compact Timber Litter, Hardwood Litter, Timber Understory) map to various TL and TU models. Original models 11, 12, 13 (Light, Medium, Heavy Logging Slash) map to SB1, SB2, SB3, SB4 depending on load level. These crosswalks are guides only — the final model selection should be based on observed fuel conditions and expected fire behavior rather than mechanical translation from the original numbering.

SUMMARY — Nonburnable (NB): Nonburnable fuel types represent areas where wildland fire cannot spread regardless of weather or wind conditions. NB classification is appropriate when vegetaion_cover_evc indicates urban development, open water, permanent snow or ice, maintained agricultural land, or bare ground with insufficient fuel. Fire_intensity should be zero for NB cells under all conditions. NB is the first classification to rule in or out before attempting any fire behavior fuel model selection. Note that urban areas classified as NB may still experience structural fire losses during wildland fire events through firebrand or house-to-house transmission, but these mechanisms are outside the scope of Rothermel surface fire spread modeling.

SUMMARY — Grass (GR): Grass fuel types are the most wind-responsive and curing-sensitive of all fuel categories. All GR models are dynamic — fire behavior potential swings dramatically based on how cured the grass is. Green uncured grass (high NDVI, live herbaceous moisture >= 120%) produces suppressed fire behavior. Fully cured grass (low NDVI, live herbaceous moisture <= 30%) produces maximum fire behavior for the given model, ranging from moderate spread and low flame length in sparse GR1 to extreme spread and extreme flame length in dense GR9. Wind speed is the dominant driver of rate of spread increase. Climate regime (dry vs humid) determines extinction moisture and which GR sub-models are appropriate. For cell_state reasoning: high wind + low fuel_moisture + low NDVI in a grass-covered cell represents maximum fire risk within the GR category. Flame lengths in the most severe GR scenarios can exceed 25 feet (Extreme class) under fully cured, high-wind conditions.

SUMMARY — Grass-Shrub (GS): Grass-shrub fuel types occupy the transition zone between pure grass and shrub-dominated landscapes. Both the grass and shrub components contribute to fire behavior, and all GS models are dynamic. GS fuel types apply when shrubs cover up to approximately 50 percent of the site alongside a meaningful grass component. Fire behavior ranges from moderate spread and low flame length in GS1 to high spread and very high flame length in GS4. GS4 is particularly notable — with 12.4 tons per acre fine fuel load, it produces some of the highest flame lengths in the GS category. Climate regime distinguishes dry (GS1, GS2) from humid (GS3, GS4) variants. For cell_state reasoning: vegetaion_cover_evc showing mixed grass-shrub cover is the classifier; curing state via NDVI determines live-to-dead herbaceous transfer; fuel_moisture drives dead fuel behavior. GS cells under fully cured, high-wind, low-moisture conditions approach Very High flame length in the heavier models.

SUMMARY — Shrub (SH): Shrub fuel types apply when shrubs dominate at least 50 percent of the site with sparse grass. Most SH models are static — fire behavior is driven primarily by dead fuel moisture rather than live herbaceous curing. Fire behavior ranges from very low spread and very low flame length in SH1 to high spread and very high flame length in SH5, SH7, and SH9. Heavy tall shrub models (SH5, SH7 at 4-6 feet depth) produce fire behavior comparable to the most severe grass conditions. Climate regime is a key differentiator: dry climate shrubs (extinction moisture 15%) ignite more readily under a broader range of moisture conditions; humid climate shrubs (extinction moisture 30-40%) require drier conditions to sustain spread. For cell_state reasoning: dominant shrub cover via vegetaion_cover_evc is the primary classifier; fuel_moisture scenario is the primary behavioral driver for most SH models; shrub height and density inferred from vegetaion_cover_evc further refine the model selection at the sub-type level.

SUMMARY — Timber-Understory (TU): Timber-understory fuel types represent forested areas where both the litter layer and the understory vegetation contribute to surface fire behavior. TU models are the bridge between pure litter-driven fire (TL) and understory-driven fire (GR, GS, SH). Two TU models are dynamic (TU1 and TU3) where an herbaceous understory component shifts with moisture content; others are static. Fire behavior ranges from low spread and low flame length in TU1 and TU2 to high spread and moderate flame length in TU3 and TU4. TU4 is noteworthy for its very low extinction moisture (12%) and very high characteristic SAV — representing dense, fine-fueled dwarf conifer stands that ignite readily. For cell_state reasoning: forest cover with a contributing understory layer in vegetaion_cover_evc is the classifier; whether the understory is herbaceous (suggesting TU1/TU3) or woody shrub (suggesting TU2/TU5) further refines selection; fuel_moisture is the primary behavioral driver; NDVI informs herbaceous understory state in dynamic TU models.

SUMMARY — Timber Litter (TL): Timber litter fuel types represent closed-canopy forest floors where dead and down woody material is the fire carrier and live fuels have little influence. All TL models are static. TL fuelbeds generally produce lower spread rates and flame lengths than other fuel types, but they are operationally important because surface fire intensity in TL fuelbeds is the primary driver of crown fire initiation. TL models are differentiated by litter type (needle vs broadleaf), load level, compactness, and presence of downed logs. Spread rates range from very low (TL1, TL2, TL3) to moderate (TL6, TL8, TL9). Flame lengths remain low to moderate across all TL models even under adverse conditions. For cell_state reasoning: closed forest canopy with minimal understory in vegetaion_cover_evc is the classifier; fuel_moisture scenario is the sole behavioral driver since all models are static and wind responsiveness is lower than grass types; the key risk from TL cells is not high spread rate but potential crown fire initiation from sustained low-intensity surface fire.

SUMMARY — Slash-Blowdown (SB): Slash-blowdown fuel types represent post-disturbance landscapes — logging operations, wind events, or heavy tree mortality — where large quantities of dead and down woody material have accumulated. All SB models are static. Fire behavior ranges from moderate spread and low flame length in SB1 to very high spread and very high flame length in SB4. The key differentiator within SB is fuel arrangement: compact, deep slash with fine fuel weighting (SB3) produces high spread rates; total blowdown with attached foliage not yet compacted (SB4) produces the highest spread rates due to the elevated, aerated fuelbed. For cell_state reasoning: vegetaion_cover_evc indicating post-harvest or post-blowdown conditions with heavy downed woody debris is the primary classifier; fuel_moisture is the primary behavioral driver for all static SB models; SB cells represent some of the highest fire risk scenarios in the dataset under low-moisture, high-wind conditions given the combination of high fuel load and fine fuel availability.
